opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most exciting directions right now. If you look at how most neural networks work today, especially large generative models, they learn the world mostly from 2D data: images, videos, text. They're incredibly powerful, but they don't really have a built-in understanding that the world is three-dimensional, that objects persist, that there's mass, momentum, collisions, conservation laws. They have to rediscover all of that statistically from huge amounts of data, and often they get it only approximately right. You see videos where a hand merges into a cup or a ball suddenly changes size.

Simulation is almost the opposite. In physical simulation we encode the structure of the world explicitly. We have a 3D representation, whether particles, meshes, or grids, and we have equations of motion we trust. It's very precise and generalizes really well, but it's hard to build, it needs a lot of manual setup, and it doesn't learn from data by itself.

So the idea of a 3D inductive bias is to combine the two. Instead of asking a network to learn everything from pixels, you give it a representation of the world that's natively 3D, and where possible you put physics inside the loop. That was a big motivation behind the differentiable programming work we did in Taichi, DiffTaichi. If your simulator is differentiable, you can backpropagate through the physics. You can optimize a controller, infer material parameters from observations, or train a network whose outputs go through a simulator before you compute the loss. The network doesn't have to learn gravity; gravity is already there. It just has to learn the parts we don't know how to write down.

I think of it as a division of labor. Neural networks are great at perception, at handling messy, ambiguous, high-dimensional stuff, and at generating plausible content. Simulators are great at being consistent and physically correct. When you put a 3D structure in the middle, you get the best of both: something that can learn from data but also respects geometry and physics.

This is also why I'm so interested in 3D generative AI. If we can generate 3D assets that are not just visually nice but also structured and simulation-ready, they can plug into games, robotics, and film, and into physics engines. Long term, I believe the most capable world models will have some explicit 3D understanding, rather than purely implicit pixel prediction. We probably won't hand-code everything like in classic graphics, but we also shouldn't throw away decades of knowledge about how the physical world works. The interesting question is where to draw the line between what we build in and what we let the model learn.

r001.rationale: The response describes native 3D representations such as particles, meshes, or grids, but does not propose sampling points in 3D space as a neural network operator.

r002.rationale: It describes a differentiable simulator, backpropagation through physics, and training network outputs through the simulator before computing the loss, conveying an end-to-end differentiable setup.

r003.rationale: It combines physical simulation with neural networks’ ability to handle messy or ambiguous data, but does not identify adaptability to complex boundary conditions.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the way I think about it, neural networks today are incredibly good at learning from data, but they're often learning in a space that doesn't really match the physical world. Images are 2D projections, videos are sequences of those projections, and the network has to somehow rediscover that there's a 3D world underneath with objects, materials, and physics. That's a lot of wasted capacity, and it's also why these models can be so fragile when you ask them to reason about things like occlusion, contact, or what happens when you push on something.

Simulation gives you the opposite starting point. If you build a differentiable physics simulator, you already have the 3D structure baked in. Particles live in 3D space, materials have stiffness and density, and conservation laws constrain what can happen. The question I'm interested in is how to put those two pieces together so the network doesn't have to learn the laws of physics from scratch, but can still learn the parts we can't write down analytically.

Concretely, I see a few layers to this. The first is using the simulator as a differentiable layer inside a network. We did some of this with DiffTaichi, where you can backpropagate through thousands of simulation steps and learn controllers or infer material parameters directly from observations. The physics is the inductive bias, and gradients flow through it just like any other layer.

The second layer is hybrid models, where the simulator handles what it's good at, like momentum and collisions, and a neural network fills in the gaps, like a constitutive model for a weird material or a correction term for coarse resolution. That way the learned part is small and well constrained, and it tends to generalize much better than a pure black box.

And the third, which I think is the most exciting, is going from pixels to physics. You take raw video, reconstruct a 3D representation, maybe Gaussian splats or particles, and then fit a simulator on top of that so you can actually interact with the scene, poke it, deform it, and predict what happens. The 3D representation becomes the bridge. Once you're in that space, the simulator and the network speak the same language, and you can train end to end.

The reason I care so much about the systems side, with things like Taichi, is that none of this works if the simulator is slow or hard to differentiate. You need the physics to run at neural network speeds on GPUs, and you need gradients to be a first-class feature. Once you have that, combining simulation and learning stops being a research curiosity and starts being just how you build models of the physical world.

r001.rationale: The response discusses 3D representations and simulation, but does not propose sampling points in 3D space as an operator within a neural network.

r002.rationale: It describes a differentiable simulator within a network, gradients flowing through it, and training the network end to end in the shared 3D representation.

r003.rationale: It pairs simulation with neural models that fill gaps such as unusual material behavior, but does not identify adaptability to complex boundary conditions.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to give neural networks some structure that reflects the physical world. If you’re learning from images, for example, the observations are two-dimensional, but the underlying scene is three-dimensional. Objects have geometry, they move, they collide, and they interact with materials and forces. A 3D inductive bias lets us build those ideas into the learning process instead of asking a network to discover everything from pixels.

One way to combine them is to let a neural network infer a scene’s geometry, material properties, and initial conditions, and then use a simulator to predict what happens next. You can render that prediction and compare it with the observations. If the simulation is differentiable, that error can provide a learning signal back to the network.

Of course, the simulator won’t capture everything perfectly. Neural networks can also learn parts of the dynamics that are difficult to model. So I see this as a complementary relationship: simulation supplies physical structure, and learning supplies flexibility. The exciting possibility is a system that can predict how a scene would change if you pushed an object or changed its material, rather than only recognizing what is in an image.

r001.rationale: The response describes inferring scene geometry and using a simulator, but does not propose sampling points in 3D space as a neural-network operator.

r002.rationale: It describes a 3D-informed network whose predictions are compared with observations, with differentiable simulation providing a learning signal back to the network.

r003.rationale: It pairs simulation’s physical structure with learning’s flexibility, but does not specify adaptability to complex boundary conditions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to give the neural network some structure that reflects the three-dimensional world. If you want a model to understand how an object moves or deforms, it helps to represent geometry, materials, and interactions explicitly, rather than asking it to infer everything from pixels.

Simulation can provide that structure. You can let a simulator handle the physical evolution, while a neural network learns things that are difficult to specify—material properties, for example, or parts of the dynamics that your physical model doesn’t capture. With differentiable simulation, you can compare the simulated result with observations and propagate that error back to learn those parameters.

So the idea is to combine the flexibility of learning with the structure of physics. Hopefully, that gives you models that need less data and generalize better when you change the viewpoint, the geometry, or the forces acting on an object.

r001.rationale: The response discusses explicitly representing geometry, materials, and interactions, but does not propose sampling points in 3D space as a neural-network operator.

r002.rationale: It says differentiable simulation can propagate error back to learn parameters, but does not clearly state that the neural architecture incorporating the 3D inductive bias is end-to-end differentiable.

r003.rationale: It combines simulation of physical evolution with neural learning, but does not mention adapting to complex boundary conditions.
